reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of liver disease or portal hypertension, arterial hypoxaemia from an abnormal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, and intrapulmonary vascular dilatations
Characteristic clinical clues are platypnoea (breathlessness worse when upright) and orthodeoxia (arterial oxygen falling on standing)
Hypoxaemia arises because dilated pulmonary vessels allow blood to pass too quickly for full oxygenation, rather than from intrinsic lung disease
Contrast-enhanced (bubble) echocardiography is the key screening test, showing delayed appearance of microbubbles in the left heart after several cardiac cycles, indicating intrapulmonary shunting
It should be distinguished from portopulmonary hypertension, which involves raised pulmonary arterial pressure rather than vasodilatation, as the two have very different management
Severity is graded by the degree of arterial hypoxaemia, and worsening oxygenation predicts poorer survival
No effective medical therapy reliably reverses the vascular changes; supplemental oxygen provides symptomatic support
Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment and can resolve the syndrome, so its presence influences transplant prioritisation, particularly with severe hypoxaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatopulmonary syndrome develops in the setting of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension when the pulmonary microvasculature becomes abnormally dilated. Increased production of vasodilators, particularly nitric oxide, together with pulmonary intravascular accumulation of macrophages and angiogenic signalling, causes widening of the pulmonary precapillary and capillary vessels. Red cells passing through these dilated channels are incompletely oxygenated because oxygen cannot diffuse to the centre of the widened vessel and transit time is reduced, creating a functional right-to-left shunt and widening the alveolar-arterial gradient. In the upright position, preferential perfusion of dilated vessels at the lung bases worsens shunting, producing orthodeoxia and platypnoea. The underlying lung parenchyma is typically normal.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic obstructive or interstitial lung disease
Pneumonia or other parenchymal lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas analysis with calculation of the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, ideally seated and supine
Contrast (agitated saline bubble) transthoracic echocardiography to detect intrapulmonary shunting
Pulse oximetry in supine and upright positions to detect orthodeoxia
Pulmonary function tests and chest imaging to exclude intrinsic lung disease
Technetium-labelled macroaggregated albumin scanning to quantify shunt in selected cases
Assessment of severity of the underlying liver disease and portal hypertension
redFlags: Severe arterial hypoxaemia indicating advanced disease and poor prognosis, and warranting expedited transplant assessment
Cyanosis and digital clubbing signalling significant shunting
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is poor without liver transplantation and worsens as arterial hypoxaemia deepens; transplantation can reverse the intrapulmonary vascular changes and improve oxygenation over months, though very severe pre-transplant hypoxaemia increases peri-operative risk.
pitfalls: Attributing hypoxaemia in a patient with liver disease to intrinsic lung or cardiac disease and missing the diagnosis
Confusing it with portopulmonary hypertension, which requires entirely different management
Failing to screen for it, since it affects candidacy and prioritisation for transplantation
Overlooking orthodeoxia by measuring oxygenation only when supine
